Second Sight

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
the world's fist bionic eye.

Summary:
It is officially known as a “Retinal Prosthesis System” that “provides electrical stimulation of the retina to induce visual perception”. In other words, it is a bionic eye that allows blind people to see.

A company in California has developed a device, a bionic eye that can restore sight to people with conditions that affect the retina. A small camera sends impulses to an implant in a patients eye and these impulses are transmitted to the optical nerve. The brain then interprets the impulses and the patient can see.

Further information:
SECOND SIGHT
It is officially known as a “Retinal Prosthesis System” that “provides electrical stimulation of the retina to induce visual perception”.
In other words, it is a bionic eye that allows blind people to see.
In a healthy eye, the photoreceptors (rods and cones) in the retina convert light into tiny electrochemical impulses that are sent through the optic nerve and into the brain, where they are decoded into images. If the photoreceptors no longer function correctly—due to conditions such as retinitis pigmentosa—the first step in this process is disrupted, and the visual system cannot transform light into images.

The Retinal Prosthesis System is designed to bypass the damaged photoreceptors altogether. A miniature video camera housed in the patient's glasses captures a scene. The video is sent to a small patient-worn computer (i.e., the video processing unit – VPU) where it is processed and transformed into instructions that are sent back to the glasses via a cable. These instructions are transmitted wirelessly to an antenna in the implant. The signals are then sent to the electrode array, which emits small pulses of electricity. These pulses are intended to bypass the damaged photoreceptors and stimulate the retina’s remaining cells, which transmit the visual information along the optic nerve to the brain. This process is intended to create the perception of patterns of light which patients can learn to interpret as visual patterns.
The device has been approved for implantation in human patients and the results are amazing. The bionic eye works and patients can see (again).

Example: “Allen Zderad was recently able to see his wife of 45 years for the first time in a decade. The Minnesota man seemed to burst into simultaneous laughter and tears as he caught a glimpse of her with his new "bionic eye." Zderad, who is 68, has retinitis pigmentosa, a degenerative eye disease that began to progress at a rapid pace 20 years ago. The disease causes deterioration of the part of the retina that turns light into vision, and eventually leads to total blindness.
Now with the help of a recently developed medical device, Zderad's vision of the world has changed. He's one of just a handful of people in the world to get the "bionic eye" device known as Second Sight Argus II retinal prosthesis system. Zderad's was implanted by Dr. Raymond Iezzi of the Mayo Clinic.”

Second Sight is the company that has developed this device under the leadership of Dr Bob Greenberg. The company is in Sylmar, California. We have filmed at the facility and also an interview with Dr Greenberg. We also have overlays of operations, implants and patients who has had their sight restored.

Press Release:


Seeing is believing
Imagine being able to see for the first time in decades. For many blind people, seeing now means believing in the power of cutting-edge medical science. A small Californian engineering company has pioneered a remarkable bionic eye, capable of restoring sight to people with conditions that affect the retina. Carte Blanche witnesses the miracle of second sight.


Script:


V/O:
Larry Hester is sixty six years old and totally blind…. He is about to experience a miracle.
UP SOUND
Everybody ready? Three, two, one…
Larry: Yes!
Wife: Can you see? Can you see Larry?
Larry: Yes!
Wife: Oh my goodness! Can I give him a kiss? Can you really see?
Larry: Yes!
Wife: Oh my goodness!
Larry: Big time flashing!
LINK:
Larry has been blind for more than 30 years from a condition called Retinitis Pigmentosa. It sounds like pure science fiction, but he can see again thanks to a bionic eye.
UP SOUND
Larry: That’s significant right there!
Wife: That’s cool.
Robert Greenberg
It is something that was science fiction obviously, twenty five years ago. And when we first started, when I first started doing research in this area, people thought I was a little crazy. But eventually technology caught up and made it possible.
V/O:
Dr Robert Greenberg is the driving force behind a so-called bionic eye that enables blind people like Larry to see again.

The bionic eye is actually a system consisting of an ocular implant, glasses fitted with a tiny camera and a small computer-processor.

Bob has been developing this system for more than twenty five years. His interest in a bionic eye started when he was a student at Johns Hopkins Hospital.

By chance a retinal surgeon invited him to witness a key procedure.
Robert Greenberg
This doctor was getting ready to do an experiment and it was actually the first experiment at Johns Hopkins where he was going to put an electrode in a blind person’s eye under local anaesthesia and electrically stimulate the patient’s eye. And here I was, a second year medical student being invited for the first time ever into an operating room. He put this electrode into the patient’s eye and the patient saw a spot of light. He put a second wire in the patient’s eye and he saw two spots of light. This totally blind patient, and I was hooked at that moment. Said ‘wow’, if this patient can see two spots of light; if we could do a hundred spots of light he could see an image. It’s just engineering. I was trained as an engineer and said I think I can do this.
Claire Link:
It took Bob 25 years of hard work, but last year his first patient received the gift of sight. His research focuses mainly on patients who go blind due to damage to the retina.
V/O:
Sight is generated when light falls onto the retina at the back of the eye. Delicate cells called rods and cones in the retina convert light into electrical impulses that are transmitted via the optic nerve to the brain’s visual cortex. The brain interprets these impulses as images.

However, if the retina is damaged through injury or disease, vision is impaired. One of the conditions that affect the rods and cones in the retina is Retinitis Pigmentosa or RP, a disease that leads to blindness.
V/O:
Claudette Medefindt is the Director for Science at Retina South Africa, an organization for people affected by RP. She also suffers from the disease and has only about 10% sight.
Claudette
It is a genetic condition that you inherit from your parents. You know you inherit genes from your parents and some genes have got mistakes. And this particular mistakes leads to a breakdown in the photo receptors, which are the cells in the eye that react to light.
V/O:
When the photoreceptors, the rods and cones on the surface of the retina start to degenerate, they cannot send impulses to the optic nerve.

First peripheral vision is lost, tunnel vision develops and this eventually leads to blindness. There is no cure.
Claire Question:
Are you going to go completely blind?

Claudette:
If I live long enough, yes. The rate of degeneration is different from person to person. But you’re losing about ten percent a year. So that little island of vision that I have is getting narrower and narrower. In some cases you lose it completely. So that thought is very frightening because even though I have only a little bit of vision, it is very precious.
V/O:
It was with RP sufferers in mind that Bob began to develop his technology at the Second Sight facility in California.

His aim was to electronically replicate what the diseased retinal cells could no longer do.

His solution is known as a retinal prosthesis system.
Claire link:
Bob calls his system the Argus, referring to the 100 eyed giant of Greek mythology.
Bob
The way the Argus two works is there is a pair of glasses with a video camera on the bridge of the nose. And the signal from the video camera, like a cell phone or any video camera, picks up the scene in front of the patient. That scene is then wirelessly transmitted to an implant that is in and around the eye.
V/O:
In this mock-up the red strips represent the eye muscles and the implant can be seen on the upper left side of the eye.

The implant itself consists of a tiny wireless receiver and an array of electrodes.

This is the device about to be implanted in a patient’s eye.

The tiny receiver is positioned on the side of the eye and fastened.

The electrode array is pushed into the eye itself through a small incision. Here it is visible through the pupil. It is then positioned centrally on the retina adjacent to the optic nerve.
Bob:
Those electrodes become kind of like lights on a scoreboard. Images are projected onto the retina electrically and corresponding to the signal from the video camera. With that these patients who are totally blind can see the images that are being transmitted from the video camera. It’s implanted in outpatient procedure, the patient gets the implant and goes home the same day. Once it’s implanted you can’t see it, the patient can’t feel it. It essentially becomes part of their eye.
V/O:
Patients do not regain normal, 20/20 vision through the device, but the pixels they see allow them to identify objects, read large letters and even to recognize faces in black and white.

And the system can be continually upgraded thanks to the design of the processor.
Bob:
The device is software based so just like an IPhone where you can upgrade the software and get new functionality, we can do the same with this. Some examples of things that we are working on in the clinic are ways of improving the resolution of the device, improve the clarity of the image, also we’ve been able to provide colour vision for patients where we’ve been able to provide different colours. So those are the kind of things that future upgrades should allow.
V/O:
The device was approved in the European Union and the USA in 2013 and implants became available there last year.

The device has not yet been approved in South Africa.

This is Jeroen Perk who was robbed of his sight by retinitis pigmentosa many years ago. He received an implant last year. At an archery centre in Holland the instructor teaches him how to shoot arrows. With his bionic eye system he is able to take aim and hit the target time after time.

UPSOUND


V/O:
As the current system is designed to provide electrical impulses to the optic nerve, it means the optic nerve has to be intact for the system to work.
Bob:
For other diseases like glaucoma or diabetic retinopathy or some forms of trauma or infection where that cable going back to the brain is actually damaged. For that we are working on a version of the implant, a very similar implant where we put it directly to the visual part of the brain. That’s kind of the next step.
V/O
Bob plans to call this new generation of retinal prosthesis the Orion.
Bob:
It will benefit patient even who have had their eye removed for some reason. Maybe they had a cancer in the eye, maybe they had a very bad accident The Orion does not require an eye at all.
V/O:
At the moment the device costs in excess of a million rand and is this expensive because the cutting-edge facility where the implants and devices are produced had to be developed from scratch as there was no prior technology to fall back on.

There were also many new questions that needed answers in the development stages of the bionic eye.
Bob:
There were like the retina is very thin and delicate like wet tissue paper. Could you put something up against that retina in the back of the eye and not damage it. Could you electrically stimulate over a long period of time and not damage the retina. Could you miniaturise electronics and put them in the saltwater environment of the body which is like taking your TV and throwing it into the ocean and having it still work. Then miniaturising it to the size of an aspirin. Could you do that kind of engineering? So there were many challenges that we had to overcome.
V/O:
But it was worth it because the implants really change lives. Allan Sorensen went blind a decade ago and his wife, children and grandchildren were present when his device was activated.

UP SOUND ALLAN SORENSEN ACTIVATION

For the first time in 10 years he saw his wife.
Bob
One of the questions we wanted to know is will it matter how long someone had been blind? It turns out it doesn’t seem to make a difference whether they have been blind one year or ten years or twenty years.
Claire link
What Bob and his team at Second Sight have managed to achieve with new technology and miniaturization is impressive. But for them the technology is not the most important thing. It is impact it has had on their patients’ lives.
Bob:
It’s unbelievably rewarding and of course the most rewarding thing is meeting the patients. It is life changing. That’s what people tell us.
Clair Question
Does this new technology give you hope?
Claudette
Yes, this new technology is amazing because that technology is replacing lost photo receptors so people will be able to read, see faces and be able to walk around. And I’ll be able to continue to see the face of my granddaughters.

Some examples of things that we are working on in the clinic are ways of improving the resolution of the device, improve the clarity of the image, also we’ve been able to provide colour vision for patients where we’ve been able to provide different colours. So those are the kind of things that future upgrades should allow. V/O: The device was approved in the European Union and the USA in 2013 and implants became available there last year. The device has not yet been approved in South Africa. This is Jeroen Perk who was robbed of his sight by retinitis pigmentosa many years ago. He received an implant last year. At an archery centre in Holland the instructor teaches him how to shoot arrows. With his bionic eye system he is able to take aim and hit the target time after time. UPSOUND V/O: As the current system is designed to provide electrical impulses to the optic nerve, it means the optic nerve has to be intact for the system to work. Bob: For other diseases like glaucoma or diabetic retinopathy or some forms of trauma or infection where that cable going back to the brain is actually damaged. For that we are working on a version of the implant, a very similar implant where we put it directly to the visual part of the brain. That’s kind of the next step. V/O Bob plans to call this new generation of retinal prosthesis the Orion. Bob: It will benefit patient even who have had their eye removed for some reason. Maybe they had a cancer in the eye, maybe they had a very bad accident The Orion does not require an eye at all. V/O: At the moment the device costs in excess of a million rand and is this expensive because the cutting-edge facility where the implants and devices are produced had to be developed from scratch as there was no prior technology to fall back on. There were also many new questions that needed answers in the development stages of the bionic eye. Bob: There were like the retina is very thin and delicate like wet tissue paper. Could you put something up against that retina in the back of the eye and not damage it. Could you electrically stimulate over a long period of time and not damage the retina. Could you miniaturise electronics and put them in the saltwater environment of the body which is like taking your TV and throwing it into the ocean and having it still work. Then miniaturising it to the size of an aspirin. Could you do that kind of engineering? So there were many challenges that we had to overcome. V/O: But it was worth it because the implants really change lives. Allan Sorensen went blind a decade ago and his wife, children and grandchildren were present when his device was activated. UP SOUND ALLAN SORENSEN ACTIVATION For the first time in 10 years he saw his wife. Bob One of the questions we wanted to know is will it matter how long someone had been blind? It turns out it doesn’t seem to make a difference whether they have been blind one year or ten years or twenty years. Claire link What Bob and his team at Second Sight have managed to achieve with new technology and miniaturization is impressive. But for them the technology is not the most important thing. It is impact it has had on their patients’ lives. Bob: It’s unbelievably rewarding and of course the most rewarding thing is meeting the patients. It is life changing. That’s what people tell us. Clair Question Does this new technology give you hope? Claudette Yes, this new technology is amazing because that technology is replacing lost photo receptors so people will be able to read, see faces and be able to walk around. And I’ll be able to continue to see the face of my granddaughters. metadata.Summary: It is officially known as a “Retinal Prosthesis System” that “provides electrical stimulation of the retina to induce visual perception”. In other words, it is a bionic eye that allows blind people to see. A company in California has developed a device, a bionic eye that can restore sight to people with conditions that affect the retina. A small camera sends impulses to an implant in a patients eye and these impulses are transmitted to the optical nerve. The brain then interprets the impulses and the patient can see.
metadata.Further information: SECOND SIGHT It is officially known as a “Retinal Prosthesis System” that “provides electrical stimulation of the retina to induce visual perception”. In other words, it is a bionic eye that allows blind people to see. In a healthy eye, the photoreceptors (rods and cones) in the retina convert light into tiny electrochemical impulses that are sent through the optic nerve and into the brain, where they are decoded into images. If the photoreceptors no longer function correctly—due to conditions such as retinitis pigmentosa—the first step in this process is disrupted, and the visual system cannot transform light into images. The Retinal Prosthesis System is designed to bypass the damaged photoreceptors altogether. A miniature video camera housed in the patient's glasses captures a scene. The video is sent to a small patient-worn computer (i.e., the video processing unit – VPU) where it is processed and transformed into instructions that are sent back to the glasses via a cable. These instructions are transmitted wirelessly to an antenna in the implant. The signals are then sent to the electrode array, which emits small pulses of electricity. These pulses are intended to bypass the damaged photoreceptors and stimulate the retina’s remaining cells, which transmit the visual information along the optic nerve to the brain. This process is intended to create the perception of patterns of light which patients can learn to interpret as visual patterns. The device has been approved for implantation in human patients and the results are amazing. The bionic eye works and patients can see (again). Example: “Allen Zderad was recently able to see his wife of 45 years for the first time in a decade. The Minnesota man seemed to burst into simultaneous laughter and tears as he caught a glimpse of her with his new "bionic eye." Zderad, who is 68, has retinitis pigmentosa, a degenerative eye disease that began to progress at a rapid pace 20 years ago. The disease causes deterioration of the part of the retina that turns light into vision, and eventually leads to total blindness. Now with the help of a recently developed medical device, Zderad's vision of the world has changed. He's one of just a handful of people in the world to get the "bionic eye" device known as Second Sight Argus II retinal prosthesis system. Zderad's was implanted by Dr. Raymond Iezzi of the Mayo Clinic.” Second Sight is the company that has developed this device under the leadership of Dr Bob Greenberg. The company is in Sylmar, California. We have filmed at the facility and also an interview with Dr Greenberg. We also have overlays of operations, implants and patients who has had their sight restored.
